speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in August of last year I invited comment from interested parties on a number of proposals designed to improve the operation and development of our major Canadian ports. The response was gratifying both in terms of the number of submissions and the comprehensive nature of the various suggestions advanced. In addition to receiving a number of written submissions, I met with various representative groups particularly from the Vancouver, Montreal and some of the major Atlantic ports to discuss at first hand with them their particular suggestions and problems.
Although the submissions received represented a very wide range of different and sometimes conflicting views there was unanimity on two basic principles. First, there is a continuing and increasing need for federal participation in comprehensive planning of port development on a national basis. In determining the federal role, it has become clear to me that the situation is not precisely the same for every major commercial port. Indeed, there is a diversity of practices that will need to be reconc.led, but I am convinced that the federal role can be achieved best through the closest co-operation with the provincial governments and even more particularly with those concerned with the particular ports themselves.
Second there is a clear need for more local involvement in the day to day operation of our major ports and for more effective communications between these local groups and the federal departments and agencies with responsibilities in these fields.
To meet this second objective, I propose to create local port authorities for each of the nine major ports now administered by the National Harbours board, namely and from west to east, Vancouver, Churchill, Montreal, Trois-Rivieres, Quebec City, Chicoutimi, Saint John, N.B., Halifax and St. John's, Newfoundland. Details concerning the responsibilities and make-up of each of these authorities will be worked out through consultation. In general terms, I can say that each group will be as representative as possible of all local interests, including management and labour, municipal and provincial authorities. Each will have a good deal of autonomy, including consultation in the appointment of port managers, the preparation of budgets, forward planning and all other important matters.
In order to strengthen still further the expressed desire of many to bring the decision-making process closer to the actual ports, rather than having much of it centered in Ottawa, we will change the system that has seen all four members of the National Harbours Board resident in the capital. In future, one member of the board will reside in Vancouver with special responsibility for dealing with western ports and one will reside in Montreal with similar responsibilities for the east.
Also, since there are major port developments on the west coast that are outside the normal activities of the National Harbours Board, but which are of great present or potential economic importance, we intend to appoint a senior official of the marine transportation administration

May 12, 1971
Minister's Statement on Harbours of the Department of Transport to co-ordinate all port developments in British Columbia and to serve as the department's direct liaison with various harbour interests. This official will, of course, be resident in British Columbia.
These steps alone should do much to answer the need for local autonomy and for shorter lines of communication. In addition, there is a need for co-ordinated planning at the national level and for a means through which the various port authorities can be kept informed of what is taking place in other parts of the country.
To answer this need we will establish a National Ports Council. It will be chaired by the marine administrator of the Department of Transport, and its membership will consist of nominees from the port authorities and, as well, from the various harbour commissions throughout the country. In addition, because inland provinces without harbour facilities have a vital interest, nevertheless, in how our major ports are administered, we will invite the provinces to name representatives to the National Ports Council. This council, and thus indirectly, the port authorities and commissions will act as advisors to the Department of Transport and the National Harbours Board.
One of the first assignments to be given the council will be the task of monitoring how the new system is functioning and to make recommendations for additional improvements. Some who submitted briefs in recent months have suggested that some ports now under the National Harbours Board should become, instead, commission harbours under the present Harbour Commissions Act. There was a wide divergence of views on this point and, in any event, much study is needed to assess fully the wisdom and practicability of such a transfer.
Since the National Ports Council will in fact be making recommendations about the total system and what ports should remain under the National Harbours Board or, alternatively, what ports might be granted commission status, it would be premature in my view to alter the legislation affecting the National Harbours Board until such recommendations are received. It is my intention, however, to announce soon the appointments of new members for the National Harbours Board and, at as early a date as practicable, the names of those who will serve on the National Ports Council.
In addition, representatives to the local ports authorities will be named without extensive delay because quite clearly the functioning of the National Ports Council is contingent upon their appointment.
I am sure that all those concerned will agree that this is a practical step which the government is now taking to ensure that Canada's ports remain strong and viable. At the same time, it ensures that private initiative is integrated in an effective way with the general objectives of the federal government which must be concerned with the good of all Canadians and not just of any particular vested interest or indeed particular region.
When I announced the reorganization of the new federal transportation complex a little over a year ago, I stated one of the purposes of change was to adopt new
principles designed to co-ordinate, stimulate and balance regulation, operation and development throughout the entire transportation system. I also emphasized the greater emphasis which was to be given to decentralization of responsibility and to the concept of financial viability through the balanced use of the principle of cost recovery. The new ports policy is not only consistent with this objective but an important step in carrying it forward.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister of Transport for having provided the Official Opposition with a copy of his statement in advance so that we might have the opportunity to prepare a reply. We welcome this statement by the minister on his new ports policy. Since his announcement of last August, all those concerned with the activities of various ports have anxiously awaited details of his proposal.
In general, we in the Official Opposition agree with the objectives set forth-to decentralize responsibility and ensure financial viability. We realize that this is simply a statement of objectives and that machinery is to be set up to hammer out the details of the program. A determination as to which ports shall remain under the National Harbours Board and which shall receive commission status will emanate from discussions with the parties concerned.
We hope the minister will be receptive to having the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications visit the ports concerned to make an assessment of the situation and present its recommendations to the National Ports Council.
We trust that any changes in the administration will not interfere with the present efficient operation of the ports and that proper consideration will be given to the existing labour force and that there will be no undue dislocation of the same.
We note that the new council is to make recommendations for additional improvements. We suggest that the council should constantly review policies and present an annual report on its findings. I would hope that when policy is finally formulated under the set-up of the new board there will be a greater measure of control than exists under the present board. I hope there will not be a repetition of unauthorized people settling or squatting on harbour commission property, with the expensive litigation that has followed.
The program as outlined will give a greater degree of responsibility to the local port set-up but we are wondering what will be the situation with respect to policy-making. It is not clear from the minister's statement who will be responsible for policy-making. Will it be the National Ports Council, the Minister of Transport or the port authorities themselves? Will the Ports Council also be responsible for co-ordinating the activities of the various ports?
I welcome the suggestion by the minister that the National Harbours Board should be decentralized so that the four commissioners will no longer reside in Ottawa. I note that one commissioner will be stationed in Vancouver, and another in Montreal to handle the affairs

May 12. 1971

of all the ports in eastern Canada. I urge the minister to give consideration to stationing a port commissioner in the Atlantic provinces. As a Maritimer himself, I am sure he will agree with me that the Atlantic ports are different in their nature from the port of Montreal and that sometimes they are in competition with Montreal. We fear that if all control is centralized in Montreal decisions may sometimes be taken to the detriment of the more active ports in the Atlantic provinces. I ask the minister to consider this point when final decisions are made as to setting up the board.
I reiterate that we welcome this proposal of the minister. We hope he will go along with the suggestion of letting the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications assess the situation, and that as a result of their recommendations, plus the recommendations made by the many people concerned, this board will soon be established.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the minister for having provided us with an opportunity to have an advance look at his statement. The announcement he has made today is, in my opinion, an important one because I think no member of the House would argue that the ports of Canada are not one of our most important national assets in a great trading nation.
The basic principle of the minister's statement is, I think, one with which we can all concur, namely, that while we must recognize our harbours as a national asset and national responsibility, there is a need for flexibility in administration and for some degree of local autonomy in their operations. I realize that this statement, in the minister's own words, is simply a rough outline of the steps that are to follow, and therefore we cannot at this point arrive at any definitive conclusions as to how these proposals are going to work.
I am glad that the minister has made reference to the need for greater attention to be paid to the management of harbours generally on the Pacific coast and to the fact that special attention is going to be given to existing problems. I cannot help but interpolate that I hope one of these days some of the smaller fishing ports about which I have been bugging the minister for some time will receive similar attention. As far as our major export ports are concerned, I think the idea of having local administrative bodies that will be autonomous except in matters of major general national policy is sound.
One of the questions that has been raised in many quarters about the operation of local harbour authorities is as to who is going to take the initiative in making appointments. This is one point that I had hoped the statement of the minister would clarify, but it did not. While the minister says that these bodies are to be generally representative, he does not say who is to have the determining voice as to who in fact those representatives will be. This is a point that I hope he will clarify very shortly because I think it is of real concern to many people. Does the authority to appoint rest entirely in the
Newfoundland Railway Service hands of the minister, or does it depend on the appointing authority of local bodies, such as city councils or provincial governments, labour bodies and that sort of thing? I regret that the minister has not clarified this point in his statement because I think it is one of the keys to any judgment and assessment of how well his proposed system is likely to work. I can only say that we will be watching very closely the developments that take place in the coming months.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Transport for making his statement available to us in both official languages.
According to this statement, the minister realizes that the situation is not the same in all Canadian ports. That is to his credit! However, he attempts to define the function of the federal government in the administration of those ports.
There is mention of sharing responsibilities and carrying out studies. In the latter case, there is rapid progress, but with regard to realizations, it is not the same thing. As a matter of fact, 100 years ago, our country ranked fourth among countries having a merchant marine, and ours numbered over 1,000 units. Well, today Canada does not own more than two, and I feel that is reason enough for a minister to wonder about the part which the government should play in water transportation.
The minister reveals in his statement his intention to create a National Ports Council. To my mind this is another gimmick within the whole gimmick. It is another agency to create jobs for certain gentlemen who are seeking a role in the administration of the country. It is true that the establishment of a National Ports Council would put to use some offices across the country, but this would also mean the employment of a few more civil servants.
Since our country has 60,000 miles of coastlines, which is more than twice the circumference of the globe, and since we have such a great number of unemployed in Canada, we Creditistes would really have preferred to learn of the establishment of a merchant marine.

subtopic: RESEARCH STUDIES ON MOVEMENT OF SOLIDS BY PIPELINE
speechtext:
The Canadian Transport Commission advises as follows: 1. and 2. The Canadian Transport Commission has entered into an agreement with the Research Council of Saskatchewan to undertake studies and research to prepare "large-scale slurry property data appropriate to suitable candidate commodities for transmission in pipelines". This agreement was signed on December 24, 1970; however, the negotiations leading up to this agreement commenced in detail in the early spring of 1970. The Treasury Board submission for an amount not exceeding $400,000 was made on July 6, 1970. Funds for the project are to be allocated as follows: $104,000 fiscal year 1970-71; $121,000 in 1971-72; $130,000
Questions
in 1972-73; and $45,000 in 1973-74. The purpose of the research into slurry pipeline hydraulics at S.R.C. is to: (a) provide CTC with appropriate technical information on the design of slurry pipelines from which appropriate costing and subsequent economic analyses can be made on that portion of the slurry pipelines system interfacing between the slurry preparation and the slurry reconstitution plants at the source and destination locations respectively; (b) encourage the consolidation of a Canadian Team to undertake meaningful large scale research and development into the hydraulic design of slurry pipelines; (c) make known, to the Canadian public, all technical information directly arising from the research.
The Saskatchewan Research Council, under this agreement is: (a) not attempting to investigate either the technical or economic feasibility of specific commodity movements by pipeline; (b) not attempting to study directly the technology of slurry preparation, reconstitution, subsequent movement of the slurry commodity by other transport modes or other related areas.
In a specific sense, the objectives of the physical research at the Saskatchewan Research Council are to study the hydraulic performance of metallurgical and thermal coal, iron concentrates, potash and sulphur in a water-base slurry in pipelines. Studies will be carried out in 2/4/6/8/10/12-inch diameter pipe test loops. The conditions under which the tests are to be carried out are to be as close to commercial situations as is possible.
Surveys of certain industries have shown that a great interest exists in industry to obtain large scale slurry technical information. Even certain consultants in related fields, who claim that they have considerable large scale data, stated that there are several unknown areas such as start-up characteristics, grade control criteria, and erosion and corrosion problems. These are areas of investigation within the S.R.C. program. Subsequent to the initial industrial survey, members of the Coal Consumers and Producers Association have shown very serious interest in the possibility of moving not only metallurgical but thermal coal by slurry pipelines, and have offered their assistance in the practical orientation of the coal slurry research.
The authority to enter into this Agreement is the 1967 National Transportation Act, Section 15.
The source of funding the project as a whole is Vote 55, Canadian Transport Commission main estimates for the fiscal year 1970-71 and for all subsequent years to March 31, 1974, from the Transport Development Agency.
3. CTC is aware of the research carried out by the Research Council of Alberta on the Transport of Commodities in capsule form. CTC. is, however, also aware that the Research Council of Alberta has not investigated the hydraulic performance of large scale slurry pipelines at their facility. The nature of these two types of solids pipelines is completely different. The research, therefore, carried out at RCA. for the future (sponsored by T.D.A.) is not similar to the SRC. work, in subject or in nature.

speechtext:
I have no prepared text but I can say we know where we are going in the north; we understand the position much better than do members of the opposition. Yesterday there were complaints that nothing was going on in the north. As usual, the opposition showed a bad sense of timing because on the day they put forward their motion in the House another discovery of oil was made in the north. It is always the same. The opposition does not know where to go, in the north, in central Canada or in Quebec.
As I was saying, we have decided that the north is not to be developed at any cost. The first thing to be considered is the wellbeing of the people in the north. It is all very well to be sentimental and talk about the traditional way of living of the Indians and the Eskimos. But at a time when the Eskimo birthrate is 46 per 1,000 because the government is providing better health services than ever before, and at a time when the average life expectancy of native citizens in the north is increasing to a point at which it is almost equal to that of white citizens, it is necessary to find ways and means of permitting Indians and Eskimos to follow a different way of life if they choose to do so. This is why we have decided to put people first. This is why we are providing better services than before.
I should like to remind those who say we are doing nothing in the north that when the opposition was running the country-and those were pretty bad times-in 1960, there were only 930 Eskimos and 948 Indians in school. Nine years later there were 3,100 Eskimos and 1,600 Indians in schools.

speechtext:
I know we have not done so well for the Indians, but we are on the way to improving the situation. I realized that was the situation when I was first appointed, which was why I put the Indian and Eskimo programs in the north under the same roof, as it were- to give the same services to each. I hope that within a few years we shall be able to give the same kind of service to the Indians as to the Eskimos in terms of housing.
Criticism has been directed toward the kind of bureaucratic administration from Ottawa which is responsible for some aspects of northern administration. We have transferred the administration of the Northwest Territories to the new capital of Yellowknife and right now we are trying very hard to extend a policy of local government into the settlements. We have founded the first municipalities in the north. Yellowknife, for example, was the first to be established as a city. We have passed ordinances providing for settlement councils and many of the small communities in the north are now administering federal programs themselves. I repeat that we are concerned with people. We must make sure that we provide these people with opportunities to work if they are to share the advantages of the general economic and social levels of Canada.
Of course, we are criticized for not doing enough. I admit that two or three years ago probably only 3 or 4 per cent of the labour force in the mining industry were native people. However, I am glad to report that two years later 17 per cent of the workers employed in the mining industry in the Mackenzie District are native people. Last year we signed an agreement with the Pine Point Mining Development Company as a result of which 21 per cent of their employees at the Pine Point mines are natives. So, the situation is not as bad. Of course, we must continue these efforts, backing them up by a good education program to give the natives the schooling they need to take these jobs.
Some social problems are developing in connection with this effort. Of course, we cannot force Indians and Eskimos to work in the mines if they do not wish to do so. But I say to the Indian and the Eskimo people that we are willing to give them training. In fact, we have trained a lot of Indians and Eskimos in schools at Fort Smith and Edmonton to work on heavy equipment or to become operators on drilling sites and so on. At the same time, even if Indians and Eskimos are taking training to do some of these jobs, I say time and time again in my

speeches that it is not only the Indians and Eskimos who have to adjust; the white man has to adjust, too, and accommodate himself to the ways of the Indians and the Eskimos. The Indians and Eskimos should not always be called upon to adopt the same methods of work as ourselves.
I am confident that in time more and more of the native population will become part of the labour force in the north and share in the benefits of northern development. However, if we wish to provide these opportunities for the native people it is necessary to develop the north. This is where my position becomes uncomfortable, because I am caught between two fires. Spokesmen for the Official Opposition tell me I am too tough on the mining industry, I am not giving them sufficient incentive to develop the north. In short, I am not giving them a free ride in the north. On the other hand, the members of the New Democratic Party have told me to sit tight on our resources; not to develop the north or sell nonrenewable resources, to keep them frozen in case 20 years from now those assets are of greater value. But what is going to happen in the meantime when there are not enough foxes or caribou or seals to provide a livelihood for the natives?

speechtext:
My first preoccupation is with the native people in the north. Certainly, it is not my ambition to sit on resources of the north so that Indians and Eskimos are deprived of any opportunity to find a place in the wage economy and have their share in the wealth of Canada, thus forcing them to live on welfare. Our policy is to develop the north in a balanced way. Even if I am caught between these two extremes, the position of the government and myself is that we want to develop the north in a balanced way so as to take account of human need and the market that exists for our natural resources. We need a new emphasis in these days because of the preoccupation of the Canadian public with ecological problems. We have to find new methods.
For example, we are doing some seismic work trying to find oil and gas. We are taking modern machinery into the tundra where Eskimos and Indians used to hunt their caribou, foxes and muskrats. Some hon. members, like the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), may laugh at this, but the Eskimos on Banks Island have a real problem finding foxes, as do the Old Crow Indians in hunting muskrats. Even though this is not all that important to the total development of Canada it is damned important to them, and this is why I have personally visited the area in order to find some solution.
I have concluded that the solution is to ask oil and gas companies and mining industries to take into their labour forces some of the trappers from various localities to advise them whether they would be destroying trap lines or the habitat of the wildlife when conducting their operations. We must develop the north in such a way that we do not repeat the errors that have been made in the south. We have developed many mines, gas and oil

fields in the south of Canada, and at the same time have created pollution problems.
The government has not been waiting for the opposition to tell it what to do. What amazes me, Mr. Speaker, is that the opposition do not realize that the problem they are talking about today was resolved a year ago when this House passed four different pieces of legislation dealing with environmental control in the north. Perhaps the opposition were asleep the day we passed the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, the Northern Inland Waters Act, the land use regulations-

I think that the goals we have in the north have been spelt out by the government on many occasions. I do not want to repeat what I have said so many times in speeches in this House, but perhaps I can just elaborate for a few moments on the kind of objectives we have developed over the last few years for the north. The government has made very clear what are its goals. What we are seeking in the north is a more satisfactory life for northern residents who must become full partners with other Canadians in developing the area and whose preferences and aspirations must be taken into account.
We must also protect the northern environment and prevent irreparable damage to it. This means controls based on research and planning. We intend to maintain Canadian sovereignty and security in the north. We must continue to encourage viable economic development
Development of Northern Canada within the regions of the north so as to realize their role in all the objectives and their potential contribution to the national economy. We want to ensure the continuous evolution of government in the territories. We want to realize the potential contribution of the northern territories to the social and cultural development of Canada. We intend to encourage development of leisure and recreational opportunities in the north, particularly through national parks and other appropriate conservation measures. Those are the general goals we are proceeding towards in the north.
I am glad that the opposition has chosen the north as the subject of this two-day debate. What disappoints me is that members of the opposition did not put forward any suggestions for developing the north. They have moved a long way from the vision of the north held by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbak-er). Although there were some criticisms yesterday, many of the members who spoke did not even refer to the north. Some members spoke about Labrador, some about new Quebec, some about the Athabasca delta in Alberta and some about the British Columbia government, but very few members of the official opposition made a speech on the north.
A debate like this is an occasion for presenting positive ideas. Although some members had good ideas, the majority did not talk about the real issue, which is: Should we or should we not develop the north? Should we or should we not try to find out whether there are renewable resources in the north? What kind of development should we undertake? Should we construct pipelines in the north or should we not? That is the kind of issue we should debate. Very few members on the opposition side will adopt this approach. That is why I decided to speak first today in an attempt to put this debate back on the rails, otherwise we are wasting time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my views on northern and national development have been expressed by me many times in this House before. Rather than go over them again, I shall review some of the philosophy of the government which prevents the implementation of
Development of Northern Canada adequate policies for development. All the minister seems to do every time he rises is talk. He is great at winding up but has no pitch. The failure of the present government to promote, articulate and advance, let alone construct, a truly Canadian development strategy for the north can and should be discussed from many perspectives. This is one reason the motion is couched in such broad terms.
Today, I would like to speak to the motion in terms of the central personality of the Trudeau government. The failure of this government in the north is not a peculiar defect, not simply a problem of priorities. It is symptomatic of the general atrophy and unacceptability of this government as an instrument of Canadian development and the public good.
There is no constructive, realistic, coherent or Canadian design for the development of the north because the government has no such design for Canada. The minister talks of isolated projects but fails to emerge with a pattern of development. This is because the government has no such design for the country as a whole. There can be no intelligent strategy for the north by a government that has not a development strategy for Canada. Therefore, this is not merely a motion of non-confidence in the Minister of Indian Affairs (Mr. Chretien) or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene), although they richly deserve a singular motion of nonconfidence, but a motion of non-confidence in this government and its lack of design and counter development strategy for Canada.
A discussion of northern development is not simply about the appendages, but the heart of the government because the destiny of the north is intimately and integrally connected with the development of Canada. To view the north as an incidental and experimental matter is not only colonial, it is a stupid development policy. For instance, the north will not be developed by some utopian spin-off of 10,000 unemployed young people being told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on Friday in Vancouver to build a city in the north. For what purpose? What will they do there and how much will it cost? How will they sustain themselves? He does not say but looks for ideas. A full recognition of the potential growth and a conscious diversification of the Canadian economy is the first step.
Further, it would be a sell-out for Canada to escape the TAPS pollution danger by the premature construction of a Canadian oil pipeline in our north. Recognition of native rights to land and adequate research on ecology are essential prerequisites. It would not take an instant for the minister, on behalf of the government, to say they recognize native land rights and will deal with them. But he has not done that and escapes in a diverse fashion by saying we will not follow the United States precedent. The people in the Yukon ask for the recognition of their land rights, but the government does not budge and does not recognize those rights. Standing up for our west coast as firmly as the government appeared to do for the north coast would be both more courageous and practical.

I have said these things, not to make a case against the government's past behaviour, but to underline the assertion that the possibility of a truly Canadian development strategy for the north depends on the capacity and equality of a government strategy for Canada. And the development of either is a function of the personality of the government, in this case of the Trudeau government. I would like to express some of my conclusions on the question Peter Desbarat asked back in 1968: "He looks fantastic"-referring to the Prime Minister-"but will he work"? Another question should be added: "At what will he work?" Will he work at putting 800,000 Canadians deliberately thrown out of work back on the job? What has he done about the face of a people pockmarked by poverty? What does he do about implacably rising costs of living? What does he do about lakes and rivers all fouled up, and air that kills, and terrorists who kill? What does he do about a land beset by internal pain for which diagnosis is conflicting and prognosis uncertain? What has he done with the law of our land which now punishes for holding an opinion, assumes guilt in the absence of proven innocence and gives such law retroactive effect? At what will he work? At being a leader who pantomimes obscenity upon the stage of Parliament.
These questions are about the three fundamental components of a federal strategy for Canada-inspiration, energy and organization. I assert that on all three the collectivity of Trudeau has been inadequate, wrong, lazy, anti-democratic and disorganized, and in the north his policies have been Simon-pure socialistic.
What has been the inspiration of this government? What are its intellectual preoccupations? I think it displays all the pretentious and narrow radicalism of its first organ Cite Libre. It is essential to recognize the importance of this intellectual womb and its resultant Utter who now occupy the treasury benches and other positions of power in the government structure. Most of his old cronies have been provided with sinecures. Harry Crowe did far more justice to this phenomenon than I can. In his article "Decline of Liberalism", published January 16, 1971, he stated:
The most striking fact about leaders of the Liberal party is that they have been obsessed with demons-
King's Frankenstein was industrial conflict, class conflict, and the omnipresent forces of darkness. Lester Pearson's demons were first the Soviet Union and then the more formidable John Diefenbaker. Pierre Trudeau has a (closet) full of demons but Duplessis and nationalism tower above (all) the rest.
King sought to exorcise the evil spirits with moral excellence; Pearson with slogans and Trudeau with mild exhortations.
Crowe further states:
Now for Trudeau. What is his Liberalism? Strong support for authority, almost to the point of obsession-(his own authority). Advocacy of democracy is-a vital one. (He talks about it but does not practise it). Most of the political leaders, in and out of the Liberal party, assume democracy. But Pierre Trudeau advocates it. (Pays lip service to it in his grasping for absolute power). He grew up with the demon Duplessis-so the Liberalism of French Canada, fashioned as a "counter weight" to "censorship authoritarianism, clericalism, and dictatorship" (Trudeau or Duplessis) becomes the liberalism of Canada.
Crowe goes on to explain:
But we won that round in seventeenth century England. The anachronism and the irrelevance are monumental.
Whatever vision and imagination this government had, is being used up in a paranoid struggle against dark dinosaurs of the Cite Libre's past. This posture is negative and in substance anti-democratic. The Trudeau government does not trust the people. What is the explanation? James Eayrs has explained it. He is a dilettante in power. He is the Walter Mitty in the cabinet room. A dilettante is one who interests himself in an art or science merely as a pastime and without serious study. This has immense consequence on the shape and calibre of any Trudeau development strategy for Canada. Leonard Beaton writes of Trudeau:
In spite of long periods spent wandering about the world, he understands very little and does not know it.
First, most of the inspiration of the Trudeau government is about the unreal world of processes and opinions, not the improvement of the quality of Canadian life. Consequently, the energy of this government is usually spent on the idea and the moods of Canada; his creation of regional offices proves his preoccupation with this area. It is not concerned with the personal needs of Canadians and the economic health of this country, particularly in the north, as the minister would have us believe just now.
The government has made great strides in a counter insurgency propaganda campaign against separatism, parochialism, trade unions and greed. Yet, this government does not even have inflation and employment targets, let alone strategies. Give them credit though, they had an unemployment target of 6 per cent and have exceeded it substantially. They have no timetable for their white paper on foreign investment, and the last draft white paper on income security is back in the cabinet. The white paper on taxation, as well as the other legislation of which the minister is so proud, have scared off up to 50 per cent of the investment risk capital in the Yukon this year. But Pelletier has had the time to write a book. While unemployment grew and inflation rose, he scribbled.
Two aspects of the personality of this government have deeply shaped its organization, its demonology and its arrogance. The first is not surprising and has obvious roots. This demonology-their distrust of the people-has clearly dominated the priorities of the government. Inflation must be eradicated, for inflation, as the Prime Minister stated, has elsewhere led to a fascism of the middle class. But perhaps that is what he wants. Every heckler warrants a lecture on the stress and strain of democratic dialogue. Police surveillance of politicians and peoples homes must be accepted as essential in the protection of our fragile democracy.
A disagreement on the tactics of protecting Pierre Laporte's life became an ingredient in the "erosion of the public will". Nothing could be more damaging to democracy than to send troops into our streets, unless it is to suspend its civil liberties. Trudeau sent troops, suspended civil liberties, and called his critics bleeding hearts.

May 12, 1971

Organizationally, this distrust of the people has permeated the government. This morbid and negative attitude has generated a kind of defensive organization that covers the powers of government and the status quo. Economic growth, fiscal sharing with the provinces, the business of co-ordinating and constructing a development strategy, have been delegated to the drones, the Bensons, the Mackaseys, the Basfords and the rest. These are not the matters that preoccupy the helm.
Second, this government has not escaped this demonology because of its arrogance. And its arrogance is monumental. After all, Pierre Elliott Trudeau-dilettante and traveller-only just got to Ottawa in 1965. He only got here as an orphan, clinging to the coat tails of Jean Marchand and trailing Pelletier behind him. That is a track record that would humble most. The Prime Minister best described his own kind of arrogance in a discussion in London in January of 1969. A student asked whether it is possible for an intellectual to remain an intellectual after he has become a Canadian politician. The student obviously touched on a rather narcissistic hangup of Mr. Trudeau who replied:
Not in the true sense of the word, no. I think an intellectual is one who looks for absolute truth and one who looks for absolute values and one who, in the face of any problem, states his belief as to the best answer on moral grounds, on philosophical grounds and who does not inflict a sense of politics into his answer.
With his absolute candour and his absolute moral motivation, the Prime Minister concludes:
The politician will water it down and say that he cannot get away with it, he must compromise or it will not pass parliament.
So, as Peter Desbarats predicted in the earlier article, Trudeau, the beautiful intellectual, will "have nowhere to go but down". However, the danger of politics to the Prime Minister's precious essence has hardly been overlooked by him or his reverent handlers.

Their dream is of a ship of state with an airtight helm, one that can be seen but not seduced.

However, it is completely inappropriate for the construction of a truly Canadian development strategy for either our north or for the whole of our country. The inner sanctum of this government is not in possession of impeccable motives or impeccable vision. This unadmitted pretention is both ridiculous and malicious.

These happenings have not been in spite of the policy but because of the policy. The policy is
realistic and does not presume that we are going to develop the resources of this vast territory by a few government directives or even a few speeches. We tried the speeches ten years ago and obviously they were a failure. I suggest to you that the policies this government is following are soundly based and will result in the most effective use of the resources as they are found.
In connection with the development of the north there has been a great deal of discussion about tax incentives, and I am confident that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) brings down his budget in June we will find that this government is still evidencing a program of support for northern development through the use of tax incentives. I find it interesting that in Russia, which is a state that I am sure some of my friends opposite might have some enthusiasm for, people who work in northern areas get substantial premiums in addition to an element of private property that is completely lacking in other industrial sectors. You cannot expect to have the necessary incentive to develop unless the opportunity is given for capital and income gains. To say that this government's approach to northern development is socialistic requires a rather peculiar definition of socialism, it seems to me.
Fundamental to the development of the north is, of course, the question of transportation. I should like to commend the government on two policies they recently adopted in connection with research. First of all, a grant of half a million dollars was given to the Saskatchewan Research Council for research on the slurry pipeline. This was followed by a grant of almost the same amount to the Alberta Research Council for the further development of capsule pipelines. The use of pipelines in the north to move fluids and gases is something that does not require a great deal of research as to its economic effectiveness. It most certainly requires and, indeed, is receiving a good deal of research in connection with the environmental impact.
The use of a pipeline for the transport of solids opens a whole, new technology which could have the most important significance for northern Canada. Solids pipelining

May 12. 1971

involves, as you know, Mr. Speaker, either the mixing of the solids with a fluid and the transporting of those solids as a slurry or, secondly and more significantly, the use of capsules which float in a liquid in a pipeline and are transported from one point to another in that fashion. The concept of developing mines in the north where the concentrate could be moved by pipeline directly to markets is one that I think ought to be greated with a good deal of excitement. It implies that it is not necessary, with respect to bulk movements, to have a surface transportation facility. Railroads, of course, are the prime bulk movers. They are very expensive facilities. If it were possible to transmit solids in a facility designed to transport either gases or liquids, we could benefit from a tremendous economic opportunity and a great opportunity for development that otherwise would be denied to us.
This government has indicated that it is aware of the technological possibilities of that sort of development. As I said before, I am delighted that the government will give such wholehearted support to a research effort in this field. That seems to typify the approach of this government to northern development, an approach that is based on an understanding of the technical requirements of that area and the desire to search out and explore the best possible technology to meet the needs of the area.
The development of northern Canada must certainly take place within the context of the development of the rest of Canada. The distribution of regional economic effort within the federal system is certainly occupying the attention of this government. So far as I am concerned, I think it would be quite inappropriate if the government were to pour undefined sums into northern development without having regard to the fact that those funds could be allocated to other regions in Canada in order to obtain the maximum development for all Canada.
I certainly do not support the position taken by some of my hon. friends opposite with respect to the idea that northern resources ought to remain unworked until some indefinite time in the future. If one appreciates what is meant by a "time discount factor", one will realize that that sort of technique suggested involves tremendous costs. On the other hand, it seems that northern resources and their development ought to be considered in some sort of sequential system that considers the needs of other parts of the country. I hope I will be forgiven for distinguishing western Canada, and particularly the Prairie region. More research must be done in that area and there must be substantial greater investment in that area in addition to that investment which has been made with respect to the agricultural economy. Only in that way, only if we develop the various regions of Canada as we go along, will be obtain the best mix of economic activity, designed to give the best opportunities for our people. I, therefore, support enthusiastically the approach of this government to northern development, because it seems to me to make the best economic sense.

I suggest that much more might be done to encourage the diversification of the economy, especially in the middle north. I am not talking only about the far north. speechtext:
I have followed with a great deal of interest the debate which has taken place on northern development. I listened with unusual interest to the minister's speech today. He gave the impression that everything was going well and according to plan, that the government has the development of the north well in hand. I also gathered that he and his colleagues are content to allow the present type of development to continue without much change.

government's integration policies and of those mining companies which have moved into the territory only to exploit the mineral wealth there, leaving precious little behind for those native indigenous groups which have called the territories their home for generations.
It is obvious that the indigenous groups in the Canadian north do not receive an adequate share of the wealth created through the exploitation of the mineral resources in their area. In addition, there is increasing evidence that adequate plans have not been made either to protect the environment and the wildlife in our northern regions upon which many of these natives depend, or to put much effort into the establishment of a basic economy which could offer them alternative employment. There is increasing evidence that the present unplanned economic activity and exploration which is currently taking place in the north is having a detrimental effect on many aspects of the environment.
We have talked about planning for northern Canada. It is nothing short of disgraceful that the land use regulations, which would help to give some proper direction to economic development in the north, have not yet been brought down by the government. The land use regulations were promised months ago and they should have been in effect right from the start of economic and exploration activity in our northern areas. I see absolutely no reason why they should be held up any longer and I now protest to the minister and this House that they should include the whole of northern Canada rather than only the few selected areas to which apparently they are going to apply.
The Science Council of Canada outlined the problem very clearly in one of their releases last year. The council suggested that we make a special effort now in the Arctic. The council went on to say, and I quote:
It seems likely that Arctic resources will soon be vigorously exploited without adequate background study of the natural environment. In consequence, there is every prospect that northern development will be accompanied by the creation of a new set of environmental problems which would have been far easier to avoid than to rectify. Because of its high costs, the current prospect is for curtailment of Arctic ecological studies, even though the present pace is too slow. Yet here is a chance for Canada to try to steer the development of a great natural area on an ideal path, a course based on thoughtful prior analysis of the consequences of various policies.
In association with the various aspects of oil and mineral exploration and transport in the Arctic, it is strongly recommended that there be an intensive program of environmental research. The first priority should be given to renewable resource inventories that would enable classification of Arctic ecosystems and define the distribution of various kinds of frozen ground water. These studies should be initiated immediately. Equally important is study of the productivity of Arctic ecosystems, particularly the tundra and the taiga. The omission of a tundra ecosystem study in the Canadian proposals for the international biological program is much to be regretted. Research is greatly needed on the effects of a modem technology on the slowly renewable resources of the Arctic to which a native culture is adapted.
The sparse human population of the Arctic makes it unlikely that development will be associated with a strong public reaction. In these circumstances a more positive governmental policy and action are appropriate.
Development of Northern Canada
That was the statement made by the Science Council of Canada which pointed out to the government what we should do to develop our northern areas. I should like now to take a little time to point out what is actually happening as far as developing our northern areas is concerned. I should like to quote what the minister said in a radio broadcast on March 11, 1971 in the program "Encounter". This is the statement the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development made at that time when talking about pollution of waters in the north:
We said about the water in the north that nobody will use it if they pollute it. We will not fine them; we will cut off the water and that will be the end of it. So we want to develop the north in a fashion that we will not repeat the errors that we have made in the south.
Here we have the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development telling us that the government has a program to develop the north, that it is going to look after pollution of the water systems of this vast area. Yet today he was boasting about the passage of several acts relating to northern development, one of which was the Northern Inland Waters Act. We passed that act in the 1969-70 session. Today, I asked him whether it had been proclaimed and he replied that he did not know. Let me tell him that it has not been proclaimed. This legislation, passed a year and a half ago, would have given protection to the rivers, streams and lakes of northern Canada. The minister has the gall to come and tell us the government has legislation on the books, intimating to the general public that they are ready to move in respect of pollution. The minister is the one who is at fault. When we pass legislation it should be brought into effect so that protection against pollution could be given to our waters.

Let me refer to some of the things contained in Treaty No. 11. It refers to terms, where it was signed and the people who were involved.
Let me refer to one pertinent section here which reads as follows:
And His Majesty the King hereby agrees and undertakes to lay aside reserves for each band, the same not to exceed in all one square mile for each family of five, or in that proportion for larger or smaller families;-
This is a very important part of that treaty. Perhaps one of the important questions to be decided upon by this government, the Parliament and people of Canada is the establishment of reserves. When I was growing up I was often asked why I was trying to get an education. I was told that I would never get any place, even with an education, because I was an Indian. I was told I would never find a job anywhere because I was an Indian. This is the kind of belief which has been festering over the years and causing difficulty in respect of the reservation system. I do not know what decision I might have made had I been a member of the government at the time these reservations were set apart. Perhaps in the context of the history of that time I might have done the same thing.
It would be a mistake, in retrospect to abolish reservations. This is not the answer to the problem. Reservations are the domains of Indian people. They are part of their heritage and the life they have learned to live. These reservations must be developed. The resources must be developed in order to provide a better living for Indian people. The human resource on the reservations must also be developed in a way that these people can participate in all aspects of Canadian life, social, economic and political. This is what must be done in the Northwest Territories.
I was very pleased to learn recently that four native people were elected to the Northwest Territories Council. This representation is still small when one considers it in terms of the relative proportion of the population comprised by the native people in the Northwest Territories. The native people represent 60 per cent of the total population in the Northwest Territories. However, this is a giant step forward. I take my hat off to the government for recognizing and encouraging this trend.

I was very interested when the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) said that the white paper on Indian Affairs was a disastrous start. In many respects this is quite a turnabout because when the white paper policy was announced on June 25, 1969 his party was quite happy to see it introduced. I should like to read a little of what the hon. member for Peace River had to say on that occasion. He said:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his courtesy in sending me within reasonable time notice that he would be making a statement, and the copy of the statement which accompanied that notice. I hope this permits me to make a reply, keeping well within the framework of the injunction Your Honour laid down the other day.
Development of Northern Canada
I thank the minister for the statement he has made. There was a reminiscent tone to it. I recall during the last years of administration under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) that a joint committee studied this issue. The wording of the report of that committee dealt with the winds of change which were blowing through the ranks of the Indian people of Canada. Many of the thoughts which the minister expressed in his statement were good thoughts, repeating the thoughts in the report of the committee.
We welcome the statement by the minister. It amounts to an acceptance of many proposals made by the Indian people through the years, and made by those who have worked on their behalf, in this party and elsewhere.
That is an indication of that party's acceptance of the policy on that occasion. I had some apprehensions at that time concerning the policy because, knowing how the Indian community would react, I felt some of the things were quite unrealistic. In retrospect, however, I believe this has probably been one of the best things which has happened to the Indian community. More than ever before the Indian people have been discussing the kind of future they want. This discussion has been carried on in the Yukon Territory, in the Northwest Territories and all over Canada. This is a good thing. Very often in the past policies were handed down and the Indian people had to live with them. I commend the government for taking this kind of approach. It is the right approach because if policies are to be made for the Indian people the Indian people must be involved in making those policies. I hope it will not be too long before there is some positive indication of what direction the policy will take. I hope the federal government, the Indian people, and perhaps the governments of the provinces involved will soon arrive at some consensus because there are a number of things which need to be done by way of legislation.
The present Indian Act is very restrictive. It is outdated and must be amended to fit the needs of the Indian people in modern Canada. The Indian people of Canada many years ago lived, and are still living, in very difficult circumstances. We are all aware of this. However, on the other end of the scale some of them also are very progressive and are quite capable of taking on the responsibility of administration of their own affairs and own communities. Such an opportunity should be provided to those who are capable of taking on responsibilities. It has always been my view that a new act should be based upon the philosophy of progressive options. The legislation should provide that the Indian people may move along as quickly as they wish.
During the recent trip to the New Zealand and Australia I had some very interesting discussions with the Maori people. There is a system there whereby four seats are set aside in Parliament for Maoris, representing the north, the south, the east and the west. This system has been advocated in Canada from time to time but I do not agree with it. I believe it would be a backward step if we were to adopt such a system now. The House of Commons must never be a place in which there is special status for any group of people. Everyone who comes here must be elected on the same basis. But on the other hand, the Maori system has worked very well. The people we talked to have said that the standard of living

Development of Northern Canada which they now enjoy is a result of their having participated in the political life of the country and in the running of the country. It was also interesting to note that they feel that perhaps their system has now outlived its usefulness. They were interested in doing away with the system so that the Maori people may be elected to their parliament on the same basis as the other people.
I have covered the waterfront here. There are a number of things that I could have dealt with perhaps, but I will end my remarks here.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ADOPT POLICIES TO DEVELOP THE HUMAN, CAPITAL AND NATURAL RESOURCES OF NORTHERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on the motion before the House my first observation is that the government's failure to develop a workable policy concerning human and industrial growth in our northland is simply a reflection of their much greater inability to develop policies to promote a healthy economy. The problems of developing our northland are so vast and require schemes of such great proportions in terms of human and economic ingredients, that they cannot be undertaken, at a time when the economy is in a depressed state and when its future is so clouded with uncertainties, with any hope that we will do a good job.
Hon. members on the opposite side may wish to take some false comfort in the view that it is the opposition's role to oppose the government merely for the sake of opposing, and that we ought not to have anything constructive to say about the government on any occasion. That is certainly not my view of the role of the opposition, but I believe that certain facts speak for themselves.
The present government has had the embarrassment of having two of its senior ministers resign from the cabinet because of disagreements over the economic, fiscal and monetary policies which it is pursuing. The fact that the two former ministers may not have had identical views on the development of our economy should not in any way diminish the dramatic impact of their resignations and the clear evidence of what great divisions exist within the inner circles of the government, particularly on the matter of determining the direction which our economy is to take in the next few years and the fiscal and monetary tools which are to be used in order to arrive at our goals.
As disturbing as anything to me is the division of opinion which clearly exists within the government's chief advisory agencies on the most fundamental issues in our economy. The Bank of Canada and the Economic Council of Canada very clearly and publicly differ over the important question of whether tax cuts are now appropriate measures to be used to stimulate our economy, and I suggest it is most important in view of the future development of our northland.
The government may find some small comfort in reverting to a number of curious slogans such as "we have licked inflation", but the realities which are evidenced daily in the business and economic sections of our newspapers refute the notion that inflation has been stemmed. Indeed, going back to the Economic Council of Canada, it has warned recently that inflation is a prob-

lem which is going to persist as a serious matter in our economy for some years ahead, and for the development of our northland this is significant. Combined with this uncomforting but realistic appraisal of the situation goes also the advice that it is going to be some years before Canada returns to a full employment economy. I do not know what constitutes full employment but I should think that a level of unemployment not exceeding 3 per cent would be accepted by most Canadians as a reasonably high rate of employment provided, of course, the 3 per cent of the work force who are unemployed are not the same 3 per cent all the time and that during periods of unemployment they are adequately served by the various institutions and agencies which the government has erected to assist people in such circumstances.
In the not too distant future, and as Canada's vast and virtually untouched supply of natural resources, particularly our great quantities of fresh water, become even more in demand by various countries than they are today,
I feel quite certain that the question of our sovereignty in large areas of the north is going to be challenged seriously. Moreover, I believe that some of the over-populated countries of the earth are going to question not only the morality of our holding such vast tracts of land which we appear incapable of putting to useful purpose, but indeed our very sovereignty over them as well.
It may be tempting to hon. members opposite to dismiss such questions, but I think we should all remember that our claim to holding so much of the northern hemisphere has never been acknowledged internationally with complete unequivocation, but rather we have fallen heirs to this land by default. I would have thought that the voyage of the United States tanker, the Manhattanf through our northern passage demonstrated the beginnings of a challenge to our sovereignty. The Americans, you will recall, Mr. Speaker, while attempting to do everything possible to assuage our concerns over the possible consequences of an oil spill, nevertheless failed to give a clear acknowledgement of the fact that the seas through which they were travelling were Canadian waters. If the Americans take the position that such waters are indeed international waters, then it is an easy matter for the Soviet Union, China, Japan and other great trading nations to take a similar view when it becomes necessary, convenient or desirable for them to make greater use of this northern route.
When one examines the pathetically reduced armed forces which this country has, we must give serious thought to whether we have any realistic capability at all of enforcing claims to our entitlement to all of the lands in the north which we now regard as sovereign Canadian soil. I believe the government could well be advised to consider the possibility of referring to the International Court of the Hague our claims to the northernmost regions of our country, particularly to the water between the islands, so that these may be clearly settled before our sovereignty is challenged by different and less impartial sources.
But of even more fundamental concern is surely the question of what bold and imaginative concepts or plans the government has to put forward as realistic measures
May 12, 1971

to develop our northern lands. The question is rhetorical because the answer is very obvious; it has no such plans to place before the House. The government's single largest failing, in my view, is that they have allowed to persist the notion that settlement in our northland is synonomous with deprivation and hardship. Under present development concepts, or rather I should say lack of them, this surmise is a logical and valid one. Surely, it should be apparent to the government that if they wish to attract to the north the human resources which will be required to develop it, they must implement a number of incentive schemes. Chief amongst these must be taxation measures which will offset the economic penalty of settlement in the north. I use the word "penalty" quite deliberately because in the present situation where the price of butter, bread and other staples, let alone any of the luxury items, is twice or more than in the southern parts of Canada, a most basic economic case can be made for tax alleviation.
Some may think that the salary differential in our northern regions is sufficient to offset the increased costs of foodstuffs, clothing and other items. This is not so, and what one must remember is that higher salaries place one in higher income tax brackets so that the net take-home pay which a person receives does not necessarily compensate him fully for the added net salary disadvantage which he encounters by living in the north.
Beyond taxation concessions to people who settle in the north, the government must consider ways of making life in the north more meaningful and attractive for its residents. It is my understanding that the Soviet Union has taken a much more progressive view in developing its northern land, and I think that we might well have something to gain from their experience and achievements. It might be opportune in this connection for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who will shortly be leaving for Russia, to discuss with Soviet officials some of the questions and problems which the Soviet government has encountered in developing its more northerly regions.
I do not believe that we shall ever have sustained growth in our northlands until we begin to develop fully integrated communities. This means that the residents there must have meaningful access to a well developed cultural life. It seems to me that if we are serious in our desire to develop the north, we cannot expect the people who settle there to be deprived of the benefits of multiple radio channels, television channels, live theatre and a modest and expanding range of the performing arts as well as all of the other educational and cultural institutions which mark our southern municipalities and make them attractive urban centres for our population. The days of developing our north on a frontier basis have long since passed and I would have hoped the government would have realized that a frontier mentality will do nothing to develop our northland.
.
In discussing the development of our northern regions, we come to a more modern and timely problem which perhaps only in the last few years has really begun to seize our attention as it should have done some years
Development of Northern Canada ago. I am referring here to the ecological problems which settlement in the north can bring about. I think it is just as important, and perhaps even more so, for the government to have on-going and in-depth studies of the environmental and ecological problems which would be faced in developing the north in the same way that they are concerned with these problems concerning the pollution of our coastal lands by merchant tankers. The permafrost of the north with its problems for drainage and absorption of waste material, and the easy manner in which the tundra can be damaged, make it imperative that before large numbers of people are encouraged to settle in the north the government should bring to bear the best scientific resources and minds possible to determine the implications of large scale human settlement of the north. Only in this way can precautions be taken to meet the problems which will surely arise. Ecology and pollution are modern terms in our vocabulary, but the consequences of our failing to give them proper consideration could well be as devastating upon our future lives as plagues and other great pestilences were to generations gone by.
In particular, Mr. Speaker, I have two suggestions which I believe the government ought to act on forthwith if it has sincere intentions regarding northern development. First, I believe the time is now opportune to make the Yukon Territory a province, and the Mackenzie area as well. It is time that the residents of these two territories were removed from their semicolonial status and accorded the full rights and advantages of provincial status. I believe that the psychological effect alone of such a step by the government would help to attract more people to the areas.
Second, I urge in the strongest possible terms that the government reconsider and withdraw the increased mining taxes and royalties payments which the proposed new Yukon minerals act would enact from mining in the Yukon Territory. Few measures could be more detrimental to the development of the north at this time than for these burdensome measures to become law.
In summing up, Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to say that I support the motion because the government is derelict on all counts in developing a northern policy, as I have endeavoured to outline in my few remarks.

speechtext:
Nevertheless, I should like to raise a few issues. In the first place, I note that in the debate which hon. members opposite made possible a few weeks ago on the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, the environmental aspects of this particular subject as introduced by the NDP amendment were dealt with in an extensive and adequate fashion. Had they listened to or even read that

May 12, 1971
Development of Northern Canada debate, perhaps this particular item might not have been introduced at this time.
Looking at northern Canada realistically, it seems to me that we must admit, regardless of the rosy-eyed vision of many of us from southern Canada, that we are looking at an area which for a good long time to come, is going to have a resource based economy. With that in mind I think we have to look at programs for northern development from the point of view of resources. Programs that are most likely to benefit all of Canada, but particularly the residents of the north will encourage resource development. There is an idea fixee that seems to be shared mainly by members of the New Democratic Party, university professors and to a lesser extent some of our younger people, that it does not matter how we got where we are in Canada. They have accepted the fact that we have arrived and that it is presumably an act of the good Lord that brought us here. They seem to think that it does not matter how inhospitable we are to foreign investment, that we will continue to benefit from it. They have taken an almost psychopathic interest in the degree of foreign ownership in the resource industries, saying that because the companies which are largely engaged in those industries are now foreign owned and controlled, the resources themselves are owned by foreigners. That simply is not true.
Premier Strom has very clearly stated the view of his government when he said:
It cannot be effectively argued in Alberta that there can be foreign ownership of Alberta's energy resources. Such resources are available for lease, license, or other form of terminal grant. Ownership does not pass to the company developing the resource. The province has and preserves the right to regulate the manner in which operations may be conducted, the terms and conditions under which any energy resource may be acquired and held for development, and the rentals and other charges that must be paid to maintain the operation.
In the federal field, Mr. Speaker, the National Energy Board controls exports of oil and gas, where and when pipelines may be laid, and the federal government controls the federal lands by way of permits or lease terms, rentals and royalties. As we all saw so clearly in the revocation on April 15, 1970, of Land Order 1-1961, the federal government is prepared to exercise its jurisdiction.
With the exception of a few instances of freehold ownership of mineral rights, the people of Canada by and large through their provincial and federal governments own all our resources. The fact that we grant opportunities for the development of these resources to foreigners in no way changes the ownership, and our governments have exercised the kind of control that is conducive to the public interest.
Another idea that seems to me to be predominant is that investment in resources is not productive of jobs, that it is not in the best interests of Canada and that some other type would be better. In view of the fact that the 1971 census is almost upon us, the figures I have to rely on here are out of the 1966 census, but I am confident that the 1971 figures will bear out the trend that is emphasized here.

It seems to me that between 1946 and 1960 the only thing that happened in Alberta that was unique to that province was the discovery of petroleum in a very large way. During that period the number of jobs in Alberta more than doubled on the basis of the DBS employment index with 1949 equalling 100. Employment in Alberta increased from 82.6 to 167.4. In Canada as a whole the increase was from 88.2 to 130.3, a rise of 48 per cent. For Manitoba and Saskatchewan the increases were 30 per cent and 43 per cent respectively. The total labour force in the province of Alberta increased at an annual rate of 3.3 per cent during the period compared to 2.1 per cent for all of Canada. In other words, the number of jobs expanded in Alberta half again as fast as for Canada as a whole. The non-agricultural labour force in Alberta during that period increased at an average annual rate of more than 5 per cent compared to 3.2 per cent for Canada as a whole. The population of Alberta rose from something over 803,000 to something over 1,463,000, an increase of 82.2 per cent. During the same period Manitoba's population increased by 32.5 per cent. Saskatchewan's population increased by 14.8 per cent. The percentage of increase applied to Canada as a whole was 60 per cent.
What happened in Alberta to create this tremendously better performance in terms of population, jobs and wealth? It is a well known fact that during that period Alberta made the transition from a "have not" to a "have" province. Mr. Speaker, the only thing that happened there that was different from anything that happened in the rest of Canada and that was perhaps more spectacular than anything that happened in the sister Prairie provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan was the tremendous investment in the resources industries that took place in the province of Alberta.
The theory that nobody is standing around a producing oil well or that very few people are standing around a producing mine is all very well. Those who adopt that simplistic approach are not being completely honest in ignoring the additional exploration activity that is being induced by successful production. They completely ignore the secondary and tertiary employment that results from the resource industries. I think that any policy that on a national basis discourages investment in the resource industries will do a great disservice to all of Canada, and particularly to northern Canada.
